measurement.happened: This week in Taiwan was dominated by the AI chip supercycle and its knock-on effects across trade, energy, and politics. The single biggest story was TSMC. The company posted what TV5Monde described as a 'new jump in sales and net profit' driven by AI chips, and within days Bloomberg reported that Taiwan would fund a four-billion-dollar Texas complex built in partnership with Nvidia and other AI players. TSMC was also reported to be exploring a separate Texas investment to expand US production, per the Associated Press. In parallel, as part of a broader US trade deal, Taiwan agreed to curb exports of AI chips to China, a move Bloomberg repeated across at least five separate stories on October 16. The chip-export restriction is the most consequential policy decision of the week because it ties Taiwan's single most important industry to Washington's leverage over Beijing. On the energy side, the same US-Taiwan trade architecture produced a four-point-four-billion-dollar commitment by Taiwan to buy liquefied natural gas from the Alaska pipeline project that Trump has been promoting. Reuters and TV5Monde both covered the deal, and Trump publicly said the US would purchase thirty percent of the output. This links Taiwan's energy imports to a politically sensitive Alaskan megaproject. In the labor sphere, the Taiwan president publicly called on Micron and its workers to negotiate 'sincerely' ahead of a possible strike, per Reuters on October 15. That is an unusual level of presidential attention for a single factory dispute and suggests the strike would hit a strategically important semiconductor packaging or testing site. On the political and cultural front, the government urged citizens to 'shun' Chinese anniversary events tied to a revolutionary hero, a small but telling gesture of soft decoupling from Beijing's narrative calendar. The same week saw Booker Prize winner Yang Shuang-zi highlighted by Deutsche Welle for exploring Taiwanese identity in her fiction, reinforcing a cultural-identity thread. In the financial markets, Bloomberg reported that fund managers were quitting institutional funds to trade their own money amid the Taiwan stock boom, while the New Taiwan dollar and the South Korean won both slumped when a chip-stock selloff hit sentiment on October 15. Investors also dialed back bets on an October rate hike after Fed candidate Warsh gave little away, per Bloomberg. In a regulatory surprise, Taiwan blocked Coinbase and Kalshi over suspected election-related betting, a move that signals the government is taking crypto's role in domestic politics seriously. Smaller but notable items included PharmaEssentia announcing new drug approvals and overseas investments (Financial Times), Delta Electronics unveiling microgrid and DC-power systems aimed at the AI era (Financial Times), and a memorandum of understanding between AV and Thunder Tiger to explore co-production of uncrewed systems in Taiwan (Financial Times), which points to a quiet defense-industry push. Polylite Taiwan and the Landis Taipei Hotel profile in Bloomberg were routine corporate items with little broader significance.
measurement.expected: TSMC Texas complex: Almost certain that the four-billion-dollar Texas AI complex will generate at least one more concrete announcement or press event in the coming week, because the deal was only reported on October 16 and the government will want to lock in timelines, partner roles, and subsidy structures before the next round of US congressional scrutiny. Chip export curbs to China: Probable that the first administrative details of the AI chip export restrictions will be published or at least leaked, including which specific TSMC and Nvidia SKUs are covered and what the licensing window looks like. Expect at least one Chinese media or ministry reaction, and possibly a brief period of uncertainty among smaller chip traders. Alaska LNG: Probable that negotiations on pricing, shipping schedules, and the thirty-percent US buy-back will continue to produce headlines, but a full signed contract is less likely within seven days. The deal is politically important to Trump, so expect at least one more public statement from either side. Micron strike: Probable that the labor dispute will either resolve with a new offer or move into a formal strike vote. The president's public call for 'sincere' negotiation suggests the government is mediating, which usually means a deal within a few days, but if talks stall, a short walkout at the affected site is possible. Stock-market and currency volatility: Probable that the New Taiwan dollar will remain under pressure from the chip-stock correction that hit on October 15, and that fund-manager outflows to private accounts will continue to be a talking point in financial media. A sharp single-day reversal is possible but not the base case. Crypto and election-bet regulation: Possible that the government will issue a follow-up circular or press conference explaining the Coinbase and Kalshi blocks, especially if trading platforms or user groups push back. A full legislative response is unlikely this week. Political and cultural gestures: Possible that the 'shun the Chinese anniversary' messaging will generate a small wave of social-media commentary and at least one opposition-party quip, but no major policy change. Defense and uncrewed systems: Possible that the AV-Thunder Tiger MOU will produce a joint press release or a small factory tour, but a major contract signature is unlikely in one week. Less likely surprises: A sudden additional tariff or non-tariff barrier from Washington aimed at a different Taiwanese export sector (electronics, autos, agriculture) as the trade deal is finalized; a brief typhoon or post-typhoon weather system affecting the southern coast and shipping lanes; a small but noticeable uptick in cross-strait rhetoric from Beijing in response to the chip-export curbs, perhaps a Defense Ministry spokesperson's weekly briefing taking a sharper tone. Things I would not bet on: A change of government or a cabinet reshuffle; a major military exercise or missile test by either side of the strait; a significant earthquake or natural disaster; a sudden reversal of the TSMC US investment plans; a full-blown Micron strike that shuts down the site for more than three days; a new round of sanctions or a formal trade-war escalation between the US and China specifically targeting Taiwan's chip sector beyond what was already announced.
emoji_reasons: The entire week's news cycle was anchored to TSMC's AI chip earnings, the four-billion-dollar Texas complex, and the new export curbs on AI chips to China, making semiconductors the single dominant story.
The US-Taiwan trade deal produced multiple concrete agreements in one week: the Texas AI investment, the Alaska LNG purchase, and the chip-export restrictions, all framed as bilateral deals.

The Taiwan stock boom, TSMC's record profits, fund managers quitting to trade their own money, and the volatile New Taiwan dollar all point to a market in full growth mode despite the chip-selloff wobble.
